articles.author: Life is Going
articles.description:
Hello everyone,
I have recently made an adblocker called IframeTube, which fixes all of Youtube video buffering, removes all ads, and returns the old player UI. It should be used in a combination with a second adblock (e.g. uBlock Origin) to work properly. It does this by using the embedded Youtube player, which is lightweight, has no ads, and includes the old UI. You can learn more about this in the README file of the repository. The project is completely free and open source.
Features:
no ads, no video buffering


old Youtube player ui


auto sets your preferred video quality


removes annoying shorts elements (optional)


lightweight



All your favorite features in the embedded player were remade:
theater mode, Picture In Picture, autoplay & autoplay button


previous and next buttons with previews for the videos & next video preview is also available for non playlists videos, replay feature for the previous button


double speed logic activated when you hold space or left click on the video for 0.5s


playlist functionality


language based (the players tooltips, settings options are in your current language)


all shortcuts are supported


works perfectly with Youtube’s single page application



Download links:
Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/iframetube-youtube-adbloc/popbfaalnmahdonefnbbogalimefpcnm
Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/iframetube-youtube-adblocker/
please note that firefox may include a bit more bugs, so if you find any, please open an issue on Github :)
Issues, source code, more detailed explanation:
https://github.com/IframeTube/IframeTube
I hope this will solve your Youtube issues and make you enjoy Youtube again :). As I said, if you have any issues or questions, open an issue on Github.
You can also donate if you like to support the development :)
Thank you!
articles.title: Youtube adblocker that fixes video buffering - IframeTube

articles.author: Walter Nascimento
articles.description:
Most developers don’t struggle with laziness.
They struggle with imagination.
We imagine scale.
And that’s exactly where YAGNI comes in.
YAGNI stands for:
You Aren’t Gonna Need It
The rule is brutally simple:
If you don’t need it now, don’t build it now.
Not “just in case”.
YAGNI was introduced as part of Extreme Programming (XP) in the late 1990s by Kent Beck.
Extreme Programming challenged traditional software thinking:
Deliver fast
Iterate often
Refactor constantly
Avoid speculative design
Instead of predicting every future scenario, XP embraced incremental evolution.
YAGNI became one of its core disciplines.
Not because future-proofing is bad.
But because speculative complexity is expensive.
Most violations of YAGNI look intelligent.
They look like:
Adding abstraction layers “for scala…
articles.title: YAGNI: The Principle That Protects You From Building the Future Too Early

When I started making music videos for Youtube, I kept running into the same problem: manually timing lyrics took forever.
Upload song. Listen on repeat. Note when each line starts. Export subtitle file. Adjust timing. Repeat.
At least an hour per video. After doing this dozens of times, I thought there has to be a better way.
So I built one. Then I forgot about it.
I spent a few weeks building an MVP. Bought a domain. Deployed it. Then moved on to a different idea.
Over the next few months I'd be getting some emails which I assumed were just recurring charges from when I subscribed to the app myself.
Another month passed. I logged into Stripe to cancel my subscription.
There were four customers.
Four people had found my website, signed up, and paid. I hadn't submitted it to search engines…

articles.description:
Hey everyone! I’m excited to share a project I’ve been working on: PardusDB.
PardusDB is a lightweight, high-performance, document-oriented NoSQL database. It’s designed to handle high-dimensional embeddings with a tiny footprint.
Embedded & Local-First: No server overhead. It lives directly in your application.
Most vector databases are designed for the cloud. PardusDB is for the edge, the desktop, and the developer who wants to get a vector-enabled app running in minutes, not hours.
Check out the repo here: github.com
I’d love to hear your thoughts, answer any questions, or see how you might use this in your next AI project!

What were you listening to this week last year? What about three years ago?
If you're like most people, you have no idea. Those songs are gone -- not from Spotify's servers, but from your memory. The playlists you obsessed over in 2022 sit forgotten while your current favorites dominate your queue.
Spotify gives you short-term recaps and recommendations, but it's surprisingly hard to revisit the music that defined earlier chapters of your life. You can remember an era, but not the exact tracks that were on repeat.
In this tutorial, you'll build a tool that fixes that. You'll authenticate with Spotify using OAuth 2.0, fetch your personal listening data, and create playlists programmatically -- all in Python.

A working OAuth 2.0 integration with Spotify

There's a pattern I've watched repeat itself more times than I can count. A talented developer spends three to four years grinding through difficult problems, earns the "Senior Engineer" title, gets a meaningful pay bump — and then stalls.
Not because they stop learning. Not because they stop shipping. They stall because they keep doing exactly what got them promoted in the first place: writing good code, fixing hard bugs, unblocking teammates. Individual output, optimized relentlessly.
The trap isn't technical stagnation. It's optimizing for the wrong metric at the wrong career stage.
Early in your career, the relationship between effort and impact is roughly linear. You write more code, you create more value. You fix more bugs, you unblock more people. The feedback loop is fast and legib…
